text: This is the payoff lesson for the entire course. Here's one genuinely realistic T-SQL report, against AdventureWorks2012: total sales by territory per salesperson, ranked within each territory. It deliberately stacks four things this course covered individually -- a multi-table JOIN, a GROUP BY with a SUM aggregate, a CTE carrying a RANK OVER window function, and string concatenation with the plus operator for the salesperson's full name. Three earlier lessons in this course each translated one query like this into one single dialect -- PL/SQL, MySQL, and PostgreSQL, individually. This lesson translates this exact query into all three, side by side, in one pass.

First decision point: string concatenation. T-SQL uses plus. Oracle and PostgreSQL use double pipe. MySQL is the one genuine outlier here -- unless a rare sql_mode flag called PIPES_AS_CONCAT is explicitly turned on, double pipe means logical OR on MySQL, not concatenation at all. CONCAT, the function, is the only safe choice there. Get this one wrong on MySQL and the query doesn't error -- it just silently returns the wrong thing, a boolean instead of a name.

Second decision point: the CTE and the window function. All three target platforms support WITH CTEs and RANK OVER PARTITION BY ORDER BY with syntax identical to T-SQL -- with one real version caveat. MySQL has only supported CTEs and window functions since version 8.0. On anything earlier, this entire query structure needs rewriting, with derived subqueries standing in for the CTE and manual rank calculation standing in for RANK OVER. Always confirm the actual MySQL version before assuming any of this translates directly -- which is exactly the point the next lesson makes about checking documentation versions generally.

Here's the Oracle translation in full. No USE, no GO -- Oracle connects directly to a schema, there's no equivalent statement to switch databases mid-script. The CTE, the join structure, GROUP BY, and RANK OVER all carry over almost line for line from the T-SQL original. The one real change: plus becomes double pipe for the name concatenation. Everything else is structurally identical.

MySQL needs two real changes from the Oracle version: CONCAT in place of double pipe, for the reason we just covered, and the explicit requirement of MySQL 8.0 or later, since this is the one platform where the query's entire structure, not just one operator, depends on the version in use. PostgreSQL, meanwhile, needs almost nothing changed at all from the Oracle version -- double pipe for concatenation, identical CTE and window function syntax, both supported natively for a long time. Of the three targets, PostgreSQL ends up the closest match to T-SQL's underlying querying model.

Lay all four queries side by side and the real lesson of this whole course becomes visible in one place: the querying structure itself -- the join graph, the GROUP BY, the CTE, the window function -- needed zero structural changes across all four platforms. Only the small, specific, individually-documented differences this course spent nine chapters building -- concatenation operators, identifier casing, one version gate on MySQL -- needed any attention at all. That's the whole course's value, proven in a single worked example. Next lesson: where to look things up correctly once this course ends. See you there.
